meta.title: FROTH-RFC-0021: Cycles as Processes, Subagents as Child Cycles
meta.author: Codex
meta.classification: Core runtime architecture — agent cycles, supervision, subagent spawning.

section.title: Problem
section.p: Today a Froth.Telegram.Bot GenServer holds at most one live cycle at a time as a struct field (cycle_state: nil | %CycleState{}). Subagents do not fit this mould: they run as separate AdhocToolExecutor GenServers started under a plain Task.Supervisor, with their own parallel copy of the bot-identity state and their own ad hoc rules for finding a session/chat. This causes four concrete problems.

item.p: Identity fallback introspection. Adhoc.resolve_runtime/1 calls :sys.get_state on the live Charlie Bot process to peek its session_id and bot_username when the caller did not pass them. This is how Froth.Headlines.extract currently finds out who it is posting as.
Structural duplication. AdhocToolExecutor.build_execution and Bot.prepare_tool_call's execution_base produce near-identical 18-key flat maps that ToolExecution consumes. They drift.

Subagent surface is unclear. Inference.Tools.spawn_agent and Froth.Search can spawn many concurrent subagents, all posting into the parent's chat_id. Narration editing is not wired across cycles, so each subagent posts fresh messages with no relationship to the parent's running narration scroll.

Supervision is wrong. A cycle that owns long-running background tasks can outlive the parent's logical intent. The Bot reaches into active_tasks maps to cascade-stop these manually; subagents do not participate in the cleanup at all.

section.p: These are all instances of a single modelling error: a cycle is currently a field of the Bot, when it should be an independent supervised process.

item.p: Make a cycle a real BEAM process with its own state, supervision tree, and lifetime.
Let subagents be ordinary cycles — just children of their spawning cycle.
Route Telegram inbound messages to the right cycle based on the message's reply-to anchor or callback payload, not based on a single-cycle-per-bot assumption.
Delete AdhocToolExecutor and the runtime-introspection identity fallback.
Keep the Bot process small: it is a Telegram session dispatcher and a cycle registry, nothing more.
This RFC does not change the Worker, the Cycle DB schema, the event log, or the tool protocol at the Worker-facing boundary.
This RFC does not give each subagent its own Telegram bot identity. All subagents under a Bot share its TDLib session.
This RFC does not attempt to deduplicate chat output across concurrent subagents. Each cycle gets its own narration message; parallel subagents produce parallel chat messages.

section.title: Core Model
section.p: Three entities, strictly separated:

item.p: Agent identity — model, tools, system prompt. Configurable per cycle. Today this is a mix of Bot.Config fields and whatever the parent cycle happened to be configured with.
Surface — (session_id, chat_id, reply_to). The Telegram endpoint the cycle writes to and the thread anchor its replies hang off. Today this is implicit on the Bot's active cycle.
Cycle runtime — the process that drives one cycle. Owns a Worker, a narration message, a last-sent message, a pending-ask if any, and a supervisor for child cycles.

section.title: Process Topology
section.p: Proposed supervision tree (app-wide, not per-Bot):
section.code:
app_sup ├── Froth.Agent.CycleRegistry # Registry, keys: :unique — all live cycles ├── Froth.Agent.CycleSupervisor # DynamicSupervisor — root cycles live here ├── Froth.Telegram.Bot.Charlie # GenServer — dispatcher, sibling of the above └── ... (other named bots, siblings)
# At runtime, conceptually: CycleRuntime (root, supervised by CycleSupervisor) ├── Worker # started in CycleRuntime.init/1, linked └── DynamicSupervisor # "children_sup" — started in init/1, linked ├── CycleRuntime (subagent 1) # same module; carries parent_cycle_id │ ├── Worker │ └── DynamicSupervisor (grandchildren) └── CycleRuntime (subagent 2)
section.p: Every cycle — root or subagent — is the same Froth.Agent.CycleRuntime GenServer. Registration uses the existing Froth pattern (see Froth.Tasks.Eval, Froth.Codex.Session):

One flat Registry keyed by cycle_id covers both roots and subagents. Cycle ids are already globally unique in the DB, so no per-Bot scoping is needed; :bot_id is carried in each CycleRuntime's state for telemetry. Registry auto-unregisters pids on exit, so the Bot does not need its own %{cycle_id => pid} map: routing does a direct Registry.lookup/2 without a Bot call.

Root-cycle supervisor: a single app-wide Froth.Agent.CycleSupervisor DynamicSupervisor (sibling of CycleRegistry), not a per-Bot supervisor. The Bot GenServer and CycleSupervisor are siblings; Bot death does not cascade to cycles. This is intentional: a TDLib hiccup or Bot restart should not cancel in-flight agent runs.

Subagent supervisor: each CycleRuntime starts its own unnamed DynamicSupervisor in init/1 and keeps its pid in state (:children_sup). Subagents are started there. Parent death cascades to children via normal BEAM supervision.
Worker lifetime: each CycleRuntime starts its Worker in init/1 with Process.link/1. When the CycleRuntime exits for any reason, the Worker goes with it.

section.title: Cycle Runtime State
section.p: The CycleRuntime holds state that today is split between %Bot.CycleState{} and parts of AdhocToolExecutor's GenServer state:

item.p: :agent_config — model, tools, system prompt, thinking, effort. Per cycle. May differ between parent and child.
:surface — session_id, chat_id, reply_to. Inherited from parent by default; overridable when spawning a subagent.
:cycle — the %Froth.Agent.Cycle{} DB row.
:worker_pid — the Worker process. Linked, not just monitored; its lifetime equals the runtime's.
:children_sup — the DynamicSupervisor pid for child cycles.
:narration — nil | %{message_id, text, mode}. The cycle's own running narration scroll.
:last_sent — nil | %{id, text}. For cost-footer edit target.
:pending_ask — nil | %PendingAsk{}. At most one outstanding ask per cycle.
:active_tasks — MapSet of background task ids spawned by this cycle's tools.
:parent_cycle_id — nil for root cycles; the parent's cycle id for subagents.
:bot_id — bot identity (for telemetry, Telegram-bot distinguishing).

section.title: Bot Responsibilities After the Refactor
section.p: The Bot becomes a narrow dispatcher:

item.p: Subscribe to the TDLib session and receive updates.

For each inbound Telegram update, look up the target cycle in Froth.Agent.CycleRegistry (no Bot call required for the lookup itself) or start a new root cycle under Froth.Agent.CycleSupervisor. See Routing.
Hold bot_config (agent-identity defaults + Telegram permission fields) for use when starting new root cycles.
Hold debounce state for coalescing rapid user messages pre-dispatch.

section.p: The Bot no longer holds: a cycle, a worker pid, a narration, a last-sent, mid-cycle-messages, pending-ask-resumes, active_tasks, a %{cycle_id => pid} map. All of that moves into each CycleRuntime, or into Registry.

section.title: Routing Inbound Telegram Updates
section.p: When a Telegram update arrives, the Bot decides where it goes based on visible signals only:

item.p: Callback query with encoded cycle_id (e.g. a stop button, an ask alternative). Decode the callback data, look up the target cycle in the registry, forward to that CycleRuntime. Irrecoverable lookup failures (cycle no longer alive) answer the callback with a no-op.
New message with a reply_to matching a pending ask's anchor message id. Look up the owning cycle via PendingAsks.get_unresolved_by_message, then the registry. Forward to that CycleRuntime.

New message otherwise addressed to the bot (mention, DM, reply-to-bot without matching any ask). Start a fresh root cycle under Froth.Agent.CycleSupervisor with the Bot's default agent config and a new surface (session, chat, msg.id).
Everything else. Ignore.

section.p: Observation: the buffering logic currently called mid_cycle_messages goes away. New user messages start new root cycles regardless of whether another cycle is already running. Parallel cycles in the same chat are allowed and expected.

section.title: Stop Semantics
section.p: Stopping a cycle is a single operation: DynamicSupervisor.terminate_child(parent_sup, cycle_runtime_pid). BEAM cascades the shutdown through the entire subtree — Worker, child cycles, grandchild cycles, their workers, their background tasks, all gone in dependency order.

The user-visible stop button on a cycle's narration message targets that specific cycle. The cascade is the expected behavior: stopping a parent research run naturally stops its in-flight web-search subagents.
Background tasks (eval:*, shell:*, etc.) are stopped explicitly in each CycleRuntime's terminate/2 callback, since they run outside BEAM supervision. This preserves today's behavior.

section.title: Subagent Lifecycle
section.p: A tool call like spawn_agent or Froth.Search's parallel providers runs inside the parent CycleRuntime's tool-execution context. Instead of calling Adhoc.start, it calls something like CycleRuntime.spawn_subagent(parent_pid, agent_config, surface_override \\ nil).

Default surface inheritance: the subagent's surface copies the parent's session_id and chat_id. The reply_to may either be inherited or set to a fresh anchor (e.g. the narration message the parent just posted). Either is defensible; the initial implementation should inherit reply_to for simplicity.

Chat output from subagents is visually distinguished by a small identifier tag — initially just the cycle's short id as a bracketed prefix in narration ([c5:a1], [c5:a2]). This is crude by design; richer UI can evolve later (collapsed cards, threaded replies, badges).

section.title: Detached Subagents
section.p: Some subagents are explicitly backgrounded: spawn_agent with wait: false, or tasks that continue past the parent's cycle end. When the parent CycleRuntime is about to terminate normally and still has living subagent children, those children are re-parented to the root cycle supervisor (Froth.Agent.CycleSupervisor). They become independent root cycles.

Re-parenting means unlinking the child from the parent's child-supervisor and starting it (or, really, handing its pid) under CycleSupervisor. The subagent's Registry entry is unaffected — the pid stays the same, only its parent supervisor changes. State, surface, and ongoing work continue as-is.

section.title: Pending Asks
section.p: Pending asks are per-cycle. A CycleRuntime that has called ask carries a :pending_ask field and waits for resolution. When the user answers (routed in by the Bot), the CycleRuntime resolves the ask locally and resumes its Worker via Worker.resolve_pending_ask/3.
The Bot-level pending_ask_resumes queue disappears. There is no longer a case where a pending ask is "waiting for the bot to finish a different cycle first" because cycles are independent.

item.p: Delete: Froth.Agent.Adhoc, Froth.Agent.AdhocToolExecutor, Froth.Telegram.Bot.CycleState (absorbed into CycleRuntime).

New: Froth.Agent.CycleRuntime (GenServer), Froth.Agent.CycleRegistry (Registry), Froth.Agent.CycleSupervisor (DynamicSupervisor), all app-level siblings. Possibly a small Froth.Agent.AgentConfig struct for per-cycle identity.

Rewrite: Froth.Telegram.Bot (shrinks dramatically — no cycle_state, no pending_ask_resumes, no active_tasks), Froth.Headlines (explicit agent + surface), Froth.Inference.Tools.spawn_agent (spawn a child cycle via parent's CycleRuntime), Froth.Search (same).
Light updates: Froth.Telegram.ToolExecution, Froth.Agent.FailureIntervention — receive a %CycleRuntime.Context{} rather than a flat 18-key map.
Unchanged: Froth.Agent.Worker, Froth.Agent (the DB/persistence module), Froth.Agent.Cycle, the event log, the tool protocol.

Scaffolding. Add Froth.Agent.CycleRegistry (Registry) and Froth.Agent.CycleSupervisor (DynamicSupervisor) to the app tree. Create an empty Froth.Agent.CycleRuntime module — module only, no callers yet. No behavior change.

Move Worker + CycleState into CycleRuntime. CycleRuntime owns Worker lifetime (started+linked in init/1) and the nine fields currently in %Bot.CycleState{}. Bot holds cycle_runtime_pid + monitor ref instead of cycle_state. Worker callbacks (ask notifications, tool-call prepare/commit, result streaming, finish) flow through CycleRuntime and it forwards Telegram-side effects back to the Bot. Single-cycle-per-bot still enforced by the Bot.

Allow parallel root cycles. Bot routing starts distinguishing "new root cycle" vs "route by pending-ask anchor" vs "route by callback cycle_id." The mid_cycle_messages buffering goes away. Debounce stays on the Bot, pre-dispatch.

Subagents via CycleRuntime.spawn_subagent/3. Each CycleRuntime starts its own child DynamicSupervisor. Migrate Inference.Tools.spawn_agent and Froth.Search to call it. Delete Adhoc and AdhocToolExecutor.
Delete runtime introspection. Migrate Froth.Headlines to take an explicit bot identity argument. Remove Adhoc.resolve_runtime's :sys.get_state path (gone with Adhoc anyway).

Tool-execution context cleanup. Replace the flat 18-key map with a %CycleRuntime.Context{} struct carrying agent_config, surface, and a runtime_pid. Update ToolExecution and FailureIntervention readers.
Subagent re-parenting on parent finish. Detached children (spawn_agent with wait: false) migrate from the dying parent's child-supervisor to CycleSupervisor as new roots.
Registry mechanism. {:via, Registry, {Froth.Agent.CycleRegistry, cycle_id}} — same pattern as Froth.Tasks.Eval / Froth.Tasks.Shell / Froth.Codex.Session.
Root-cycle supervisor placement. App-wide sibling of the Bot, not owned by the Bot. Bot death does not cascade to cycles.
Registry scoping. One flat Registry keyed by cycle_id. Per-Bot scoping is unnecessary (cycle_ids are DB-unique; bot_id lives in cycle state).
Tool-execution context shape. Use a %CycleRuntime.Context{} struct carrying agent_config, surface, and runtime_pid.
Debounce. Stays on the Bot, pre-dispatch. Debounce resolution starts a new root cycle.

How does Failure Intervention surface from inside a subagent cycle attribute itself — does its [Carry on] [Stop] prompt say "subagent failed" vs "your tool failed"? UI detail; resolve during the subagent step.

section.title: Future Direction: Bot as Session Dispatcher
section.p: Once cycles are supervised processes, the Bot GenServer's remaining job is narrow: receive TDLib updates for one session, look up static bot config from app env, route to cycles. None of that is bot-shaped — it is session-shaped. A bot in Froth is mostly an identity (bot_username, default agent config, permission flags), which is static configuration, not a process.

A plausible future refactor collapses the Bot GenServer into a Froth.Telegram.SessionDispatcher — one process per TDLib session, whose entire job is dispatch. Bot identity becomes a module that reads Application.fetch_env!(:froth, Froth.Telegram.Bot). Debounce moves to per-conversation processes keyed by {session_id, chat_id}.

This RFC does not undertake that refactor. The Bot GenServer remains as the dispatcher and is simply kept small. Dissolving the Bot process on top of cycle extraction would entangle the TDLib-subscription shape with the cycle work; one structural move at a time.

section.title: Implementation Status
section.p: Implemented (as of this writing):

item.p: Step 1 — scaffolding: Froth.Agent.CycleRegistry, Froth.Agent.CycleSupervisor, Froth.Agent.CycleRuntime module.

Step 2 — Worker + all per-cycle live state (narration, last_sent, awaiting_user_input?, active_tasks, bot_config snapshot, chat_id, reply_to) live on CycleRuntime. Worker tool_executor points at the runtime. Tool prepare/commit/execute handlers moved off the Bot. %Bot.CycleState{} is a 5-field handle.
Step 3 — parallel root cycles: every inbound user message starts its own cycle; mid_cycle_messages buffering is gone.

Step 4 — CycleRuntime.spawn_subagent/2 exists; each runtime has its own child DynamicSupervisor. Inference.Tools.spawn_agent and Froth.Search don't use the child-sup path today — spawn_agent is fire-and-forget and starts its delegated cycle as an independent root (matching the old Task-supervised Adhoc behavior). Froth.Search was not touched in this pass; it still uses Agent.run/2 directly.

Step 5 — Froth.Agent.Adhoc and Froth.Agent.AdhocToolExecutor are deleted. Froth.Headlines and Froth.Agent.run_adhoc build cycles directly and drive them via CycleRuntime.run_to_completion/1; the :sys.get_state runtime introspection hack is gone.

Step 6 — tool-execution context is now a %CycleRuntime.Context{} struct wrapping %Bot.Config{}, %Agent.Surface{} (new), %CycleRuntime.View{} (new), %ToolUse{}, plus cycle_id/cycle/spam/projected system_prompt+tool_specs. Seven slots, all structured. ToolExecution and FailureIntervention pattern-match on the hierarchy instead of reading execution[:key].

section.p: Not yet done:

item.p: Step 7 — subagent re-parenting. Side-stepped for spawn_agent by starting subagents as independent roots (so they trivially outlive the parent). If we later want "user stops parent → cascade to subagents," that becomes explicit code via parent_cycle_id registry lookup rather than BEAM supervision.
The original Froth.Search migration is no longer applicable because that subsystem was removed. Current spawn_agent delegation still does not use the child-supervisor path.

section.p: Current architecture has diverged further from the original topology. Root cycles are supervised under each Bot's private cycle supervisor rather than one app-wide CycleSupervisor; spawn_agent starts a bot-owned root carrying parent_cycle_id rather than using the parent runtime's child supervisor; and the Bot still owns queueing and pending-ask resume behavior. The cycle-process extraction remains substantial, but the final routing and child-lifetime design is not implemented as proposed.

section.title: Conclusion
section.p: Cycles are the unit of agent work. They have a natural tree structure (subagents branch off parents). Modelling them as independent supervised processes rather than as fields on a single Bot GenServer resolves four concrete pains — identity introspection, Adhoc duplication, subagent chat surface, manual cleanup — in one structural move. The payoff is a codebase where the subagent and the root cycle are the same thing, the Bot process is small, and stop-and-crash semantics follow BEAM defaults instead of hand-written cascades.
